title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision but committed to it
prompt: Tell me about a time a group chose a different approach after you raised a concern. Explain how you decided whether to support the decision, set a boundary or escalate, and what you did next. You should not support an unsafe or unethical instruction simply because the group chose it.
blurb: Disagree & commit: did they voice a real, reasoned dissent AND then genuinely back the decision — not sandbag it?

rubric.label: Situation & the decision
rubric.description: Explains the choice, their concern and the group’s reasoning using the information available at the time.

rubric.label: Quality of the disagreement
rubric.description: Describes how they raised the concern with relevant reasons or evidence through an appropriate channel.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Explains their specific next action: supporting a reasonable decision, agreeing a review point, maintaining a justified boundary or escalating a serious concern.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes the outcome and their contribution honestly, including a partial or unsuccessful result; compliance and agreement are not required.

rubric.label: Reflection & maturity
rubric.description: Distinguishes a reasonable difference of preference from a concern that warrants challenge, refusal or escalation and identifies what would change their view.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore what happens after a group does not choose the candidate’s preferred approach. A sound response may be to support a reasonable decision, seek a review point or decline and escalate an unsafe or unethical instruction. Assess accountable follow-through and judgment rather than obedience or emotional agreement.
model_points: Explains the competing approaches fairly and identifies the actual point of disagreement.
Raises a concrete concern through a suitable channel, using evidence or a clear principle.
Distinguishes an ordinary tradeoff from a safety, ethical or scope concern.
Describes constructive support for a reasonable decision or a justified boundary and appropriate escalation.
Reports what happened without treating being proved right or winning agreement as the goal.
Explains how new evidence, a review point or the experience changed their approach.

probes.trigger: the reason for disagreement is unclear
probes.question: What specific concern did you raise?

probes.trigger: candidate treats commitment as automatic compliance
probes.question: What would make you unable to support that decision?
What did you do after the decision was made?

red_flags: Conceals a known serious risk to preserve group agreement.
Sabotages work while claiming to support an otherwise reasonable agreed plan.
Insists an unsafe or unethical action is acceptable solely because a senior person requested it.
follow_ups: What evidence would justify revisiting the decision?
What distinguishes a preference from a boundary you should maintain?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. My study group chose a simple poster over the interactive display I preferred. I raised the risk that our explanation might be unclear, but agreed the poster fit our time. I helped draft it and suggested a short check with another group. Their questions showed one missing explanation, which we added. I could support the decision because it was reasonable and safe, even though it was not my first choice.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
